title: What Is the Bible, and Can We Trust It?
subtitle: Three faithful answers to the question of how Scripture is true.
triageNote: The authority and inspiration of Scripture sit very close to the heart of the faith. To follow Jesus is to receive a book as the word of God, and you cannot remove that book without removing the floor everyone is standing on. But the in-house debate over the exact nature of inerrancy, over precisely how Scripture is without error, is a different matter. That debate is what divides faithful churches from one another. It runs between people who pray together, who share the same Lord, who would each die for the trustworthiness of the Bible. Hold the first thing tightly. Hold the second thing honestly, and hold your neighbor gently.
question: When a Christian says the Bible is true, what is being claimed. Is the claim that every sentence, including its remarks about the age of a city or the order of an event, is exactly accurate the way a modern reference book would be. Or is the claim that the Bible never fails to deliver what God gave it to deliver, while it speaks in the ordinary words of ordinary people in the ancient world. Behind that lies a deeper question still. Where does the Bible's authority come from, and how are we meant to read it so that we hear God and not merely ourselves.
whyItMatters:
If you have just begun to follow Jesus, you have probably already met the pressure. A friend says the Bible is full of contradictions. A documentary says it was edited by power-hungry men centuries later. A quiet voice in your own chest, late at night, asks whether you have built your life on a book you cannot defend. This is not a side issue for the curious. It is the ground under your feet.

Here is what each of these positions is trying to protect, and that is the kindest way to understand them. They are all guarding something precious. One is guarding the idea that God does not make mistakes and neither does the book He breathed out. One is guarding the idea that God spoke through real human beings in a real century, and that this does not make the book less holy but more astonishing. One is guarding the idea that the book was never meant to be read alone in a vacuum, that it came to us inside a worshiping community that learned how to read it.

You will be a better reader of Scripture, and a kinder member of the church, if you can see the love inside each of these views before you ever weigh them against each other. Most fights about the Bible are really two people defending the same Lord while accusing each other of betraying Him.

positions.name: Detailed inerrancy
positions.inOneLine: The Bible is without any error in everything it affirms, including its statements about history and the natural world, because God Himself is its ultimate author.
positions.bestCase:
Let me begin with God and not with the book, because that is where this view begins. God cannot lie and God does not err. When we say the Bible is breathed out by God, we are saying its origin is in a perfect mind. So the question is simple and unavoidable. Would a perfect God breathe out a book that contains real mistakes. We do not think He would, and we do not think He did.

First, let me define the words I am using, because they matter. Revelation means God making known what we could never have figured out on our own, God lifting the veil. Inspiration is the term for how God produced Scripture, not by dictating to passive secretaries but by so guiding real authors, with their own styles and tears and vocabularies, that what they freely wrote was exactly what He intended. We call this plenary verbal inspiration. Verbal means it reaches down to the actual words, not just the general ideas. Plenary means full, all of it, not only the parts about salvation. Inerrancy is the result. Inerrancy means that Scripture, in everything it actually affirms, tells the truth and does not mislead.

Notice the careful phrase, in everything it actually affirms. We are not saying the Bible speaks like a science textbook. When it says the sun rose, that is ordinary human speech and it is perfectly true, the same way your weather app says sunrise. We allow for round numbers, for quotations that capture the sense rather than the exact words, for the ordinary ways people have always talked. The 1978 Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy, which many of us regard as the clearest summary of this position, says exactly this. Inerrancy is not wooden literalism. It is the conviction that when you understand what a passage is genuinely asserting, that assertion is true, whether it concerns the resurrection or the reign of a king.

Why hold the line here. Because once you grant that the Bible errs in the small things you can check, you have handed the reader a pair of scissors. Now I decide which parts are reliable. Now the book sits under my judgment rather than over it. B. B. Warfield put it that the Bible's trustworthiness is a single woven garment, that you cannot cut a thread in the corner without the whole thing unraveling in your hands. We would rather trust the One who breathed it than trust ourselves to grade Him.

So when you read your Bible, read it as a word you can lean your whole weight on. Not a word that is mostly right. A word that, rightly understood, does not fail you anywhere, because the God behind it does not fail you anywhere.
advocates: the framers of the 1978 Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy

positions.name: Infallibility
positions.inOneLine: Scripture will never fail in what it teaches for faith and life, while its descriptions of nature and history speak in the ordinary language and assumptions of the people God used to write it.
positions.bestCase:
I want to start by agreeing with my brothers and sisters who hold detailed inerrancy about almost everything that matters. The Bible is the word of God. It is true. It will not lead you astray on a single thing it was given to teach you. I am not a skeptic standing outside the church throwing stones. I am inside, on my knees, trusting this book with my life. So please hear my concern as a family concern.

Let me define my key word. Infallibility means incapable of failing. A guide who is infallible is a guide who will never once steer you wrong on the road you actually need to walk. That is what I claim for Scripture. It is wholly trustworthy and it will never fail in what it teaches for faith and life, for who God is, for what He has done in Christ, for how we are saved, for how we are to live.

Here is where I differ, and it is a difference of emphasis more than enmity. When God chose to speak, He chose to speak through Isaiah and Luke and Paul, real people embedded in the assumptions of their century. They described the world as it appeared to them and to their first readers, with the sky as a dome and the earth as the still center and a mustard seed as the smallest of seeds. I do not think God paused to correct their ancient picture of the cosmos before letting them preach the gospel through it. That was not the point. The Bible was not given to settle astronomy or to function as a record of exact chronology. It was given to bring me to God. To demand that it never reflect the ordinary, time-bound assumptions of its writers is, I think gently, to ask it to be a kind of book it never claimed to be.

The Dutch theologian G. C. Berkouwer and the American Donald Bloesch, along with a long strand of British evangelicals, helped me see that this is not a lowering of Scripture but a taking-seriously of how God actually chose to give it. The wonder is not that God dictated a timeless encyclopedia. The wonder is that God stooped, the way He stooped in the manger, and spoke our cramped human language without ceasing to speak the truth. When two accounts of the same event differ in a small detail, I do not feel the floor tilt. I think, these are real witnesses, and God meant for me to have their testimony, not a flattened official transcript.

So read your Bible expecting it to do what it was sent to do. Expect it to be utterly reliable about God and your soul and the way home. Do not put a weight on its incidental details that it was never built to carry, and you will find your trust grows steadier, not weaker, the longer you live with it.

positions.name: The confessional and catholic view
positions.inOneLine: Scripture is the inspired and authoritative word of God, received and rightly read within the church and its rule of faith, neither a modern science textbook nor a flat rulebook.
positions.bestCase:
Let me ask you a question before I make my case. Where did your Bible come from. Not the printing press, but the table of contents. Who decided that there are sixty-six books, or seventy-three in my tradition, and that the Gospel of Thomas is left outside. The answer is that the church received these books, over generations, in worship and prayer and hard argument. The book did not fall from the sky bound in leather. It was gathered by the same Spirit who breathed it, working through a community.

Let me define a few terms warmly. The canon is the list of books the church recognized as Scripture, from a Greek word meaning a measuring rod, the standard. The autographs are the original manuscripts, the first copies the apostles and prophets actually wrote, which we no longer possess. And the rule of faith is the short summary of the gospel, close to what you say in the Apostles Creed, that the early Christians used as the lens for reading everything else. My tradition, which includes the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches and many who simply take the ancient church seriously, holds that you cannot tear Scripture out of the community that received it and read it well.

Now, I share fully the conviction that the authority of Scripture is real and total. But I want to locate it precisely. The authority of Scripture is the authority of God exercised through it. The book is not a separate little sovereign sitting beside God. It is the instrument of His voice. So the question is never simply, what does the verse say, as if I could answer that alone in my room with no help. The question is, what is God saying through this text to His people, and the people of God across twenty centuries are part of how I hear it rightly.

This guards against two errors at once. It guards against turning the Bible into a science manual, because the church never read Genesis to learn geology, it read Genesis to learn that one good God made everything and called it good. And it guards against turning the Bible into a flat rulebook, a collection of detached commands I can wield however I like, because the church reads every command in the light of Christ, who is the center and the key. Tradition here is not a rival to Scripture. It is the memory of the family, the accumulated wisdom of how this book has been read by the saints and martyrs who handed it to me.

So when you open your Bible, know that you are not the first to read it, and that is good news. You are joining a long table. Read it as the church's book, prayed and sung and argued over for two thousand years, and you will be far less likely to make it say whatever your moment wants it to say.
advocates: figures who stress that the authority of Scripture is the authority of God exercised through it

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Shared, claimed most strongly by detailed inerrancy
biblicalEvidence.summary: All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness. This is the foundation text for inspiration, the claim that the very source of Scripture is the mouth of God.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is hard for no one in the sense that all three affirm it, but it is hardest for detailed inerrancy to use as a proof, because the verse defines the purpose of Scripture as making us complete for good works, which is faith and life, not history and science.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Infallibility reads this verse as proving exactly its point, that Scripture is breathed out by God for the purpose of righteousness, which is the very thing it is infallible about. The confessional view notes that Paul says this to Timothy about the Scriptures Timothy was taught from childhood, that is, received within a community of faith, not handed a closed list in the abstract.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Shared, claimed most strongly by detailed inerrancy
biblicalEvidence.summary: No prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit. This describes the how of inspiration, the Spirit carrying human authors along.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: The phrase men spoke is hard for the most mechanical idea of dictation, because it preserves that real men, with real voices, did the speaking. The Spirit carried them, He did not replace them.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Infallibility loves the word carried, like a ship carried by wind, because the ship is still a real ship with a real shape, which is its whole point about human language. The confessional view reads carried along as a communal and ongoing work of the Spirit, the same Spirit who later carried the church to recognize which writings were prophetic.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Jesus says, in passing, that Scripture cannot be broken. For this view it is decisive that the Lord Himself treats even a small grammatical point of an Old Testament verse as unbreakable.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is hard for the views that allow incidental imprecision, since Jesus here leans His argument on a single word of the text and calls Scripture unbreakable.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Infallibility answers that cannot be broken means cannot fail to accomplish its purpose, cannot be nullified, which is a claim about reliability and not about scientific precision. The confessional view notes that Jesus is reading Scripture within a living interpretive practice, drawing out an unexpected meaning the way a rabbi would, which shows that the text lives inside a tradition of reading.

biblicalEvidence.summary: The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul. The testimony of the Lord is sure, making wise the simple. All three views cherish this verse, and it sits at the seam between them.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is gently hard for detailed inerrancy because the perfection praised here is moral and life-giving, perfect for reviving the soul, not described as factual precision about the world.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Detailed inerrancy reads perfect as flawless without qualification, including in every affirmation. Infallibility reads perfect as perfectly suited to its saving purpose. The confessional view reads the whole psalm as moving from the heavens declaring God to the law reviving the soul, two books, creation and Scripture, each read within worship.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Jesus says that not the smallest letter or stroke of a pen will pass from the law until all is accomplished. This is taken to show the permanence and precision of even the tiniest details of Scripture.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is hard for any view that treats parts of the law as merely time-bound, since Jesus affirms its enduring authority down to the stroke of a pen.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Infallibility points to the phrase until all is accomplished, arguing that Jesus is speaking about the law being fulfilled in Him, a statement about purpose and destiny rather than textual exactness. The confessional view reads this within Jesus reinterpreting the law throughout the Sermon on the Mount, showing that the smallest stroke endures precisely as He, the church's Lord, teaches the church to read it.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Jesus prays, Sanctify them in the truth, your word is truth. The accent falls on the word as the instrument that makes people holy, which is the heart of what the infallibility view says Scripture is for.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is hard for a narrowly factual definition of truth, because here truth is the power that sanctifies, that sets a person apart for God, a relational and saving truth.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Detailed inerrancy answers that a word which sanctifies must itself be wholly true, that sanctifying power and total truthfulness are not rivals but the same thing. The confessional view notes that this prayer is for the church, them, and that the word does its sanctifying work in the gathered, sent community Jesus is praying for.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Luke describes his own method, that he investigated everything carefully, having followed the accounts of eyewitnesses, so that Theophilus may have certainty. This shows an inspired author working like a careful human historian.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: This is genuinely hard for any idea that inspiration bypasses human research, since Luke tells us he did ordinary careful work, sifting sources, to produce his Gospel.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Detailed inerrancy welcomes this, arguing that God's superintending of Luke's careful research is exactly how inspiration produces an inerrant result, providence working through diligence. The confessional view reads it as proof that the Gospel arose from and for a community of testimony, eyewitnesses handing on what they saw to the church.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Paul tells the church to stand firm and hold to the traditions taught by him, whether by his spoken word or by his letter. Here the apostolic message is carried both in writing and in living teaching held by the church.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is hard for any view that treats the written text as the only channel of God's authoritative word, since Paul places spoken tradition and written letter side by side.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Detailed inerrancy answers that the apostolic spoken word was eventually deposited in the New Testament writings, so the written Scripture is the secure form of that same teaching for us today. Infallibility agrees that the church holds the message, while insisting the writings remain the standard by which any later tradition is tested.

biblicalEvidence.summary: No prophecy of Scripture comes from someone's own private interpretation. For this view the verse warns that Scripture is not for the lone individual to bend at will, but is read rightly within the people of God.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: It is hard for a do-it-yourself reading of the Bible, the idea that I and my Bible alone are a sufficient court, since Peter denies that prophecy is a matter of private interpretation.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Detailed inerrancy and infallibility both note that the verse is most naturally about the origin of prophecy, that the prophets did not make it up themselves, rather than about who is allowed to interpret it now. They affirm that Scripture is clear enough that an ordinary believer, helped by the Spirit, can read and understand it.

weighing:
Here is my own judgment, offered as a fellow reader and not as a settled verdict you must sign. Take it as one pastor thinking out loud, the kind of thing I would say to you across a kitchen table, not a ruling from a council.

I find that these three views agree on far more than they divide over, and that most of their quarrel is about what kind of book the Bible is, not about whether it is true. All three confess that God breathed it out, that it carries His authority, that it will not fail the person who trusts it. When I read the detailed inerrancy view closely, I notice it already grants nearly everything the others want, round numbers, ordinary speech, the phenomena of how things look. When I read the infallibility view closely, I notice it is not lowering Scripture at all but guarding the strangeness of how God actually chose to speak, through real people in a real century. The distance between the first two is often smaller than the heat of the argument suggests.

What the confessional view adds, and what I think both of the others sometimes forget, is the simple fact that none of us received the Bible alone. Someone handed it to us. A community decided which books belonged long before we were born, prayed over it, sang it, died for it, and taught us how to read it without making it a mirror for our own age. I cannot read the table of contents off the floor of a closed room. That humbles me, and I think humility is the right posture for a creature holding the word of his Maker.

If you pressed me, I would say this. I want to hold the highest possible view of Scripture's truthfulness, trusting that what God says is so. I also want to hold it the way the infallibility writers urge, attentive to how God stooped to human speech, and the way the confessional writers urge, inside the church that received the book. I do not think you must choose one of these against the other two to be a faithful Christian. I think you must love the book, read it on its own terms, and let it read you.
charitableDisagreement:
If you land on detailed inerrancy, the others want you to hear that some of your brothers and sisters who decline the word inerrant are not on a slippery slope to unbelief. Many of them defend Scripture's truth with their lives, and they decline the word only because they fear it makes promises the Bible never made about itself. If you land on infallibility or the confessional view, the inerrantists want you to hear that the line they are defending has, in history, been the first thing to go when a church begins to drift, and that their carefulness is love, not fear. Each side is guarding a real treasure, and each can name a real danger the others run.

So is this a hill to die on. The authority and inspiration of Scripture, yes, in the sense that to surrender them is to surrender the faith itself. But the exact theory of how Scripture is without error, the in-house quarrel between inerrancy and infallibility and the confessional reading, is not a hill to die on and not a wall to build between believers. It is a conversation faithful churches have always had around the same table, holding the same Bible, worshiping the same Lord. Defend the book with everything you have. Defend your theory of the book with a much lighter hand, and keep your arm around the brother who reads it a little differently than you do.

relatedDebates.topic: How the church received the canon
relatedDebates.note: The canon is the recognized list of books that count as Scripture. The deeper question is whether the church created the canon or merely recognized books that already carried God's authority, the way you recognize a friend's voice rather than assigning it. How you answer shapes how much weight you give the community that handed you your Bible.

relatedDebates.topic: The role of tradition in reading Scripture
relatedDebates.note: Tradition here means the church's long memory of how this book has been read. Some treat tradition as a second source alongside Scripture, some as a servant that helps us read Scripture rightly, some as a danger that can bury the text under human additions. Where you stand here flows directly from which view of Scripture above feels most like home.

Because we no longer have the autographs, the original manuscripts, every Bible you hold is a translation. Some translations aim word for word, some aim thought for thought, and the choice quietly shapes what you hear. A high view of Scripture does not settle which method is best, and good translations of every kind serve the church well.
